r: The applied work is foundational visual problem-solving: idea generation, concept development, and executing layout and composition for print and screen media using standard design software. These map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively and Working with Computers activities, and design-production tasks of exactly this kind sit in the highly exposed band, since observed-usage data shows creative and office-document generation among the most common AI applications and generative layout tools already draft competent compositions. What holds the near-term rating down is the course's role as foundational scaffolding for the entire communication-design sequence: later courses in typography, interface, and systems presuppose this conceptual vocabulary, so students still need it to direct and judge machine output. Diffusion also lags capability, with Census data indicating fewer than a fifth of firms had adopted AI by end-2025. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role, not any licensure lock, which is absent here.

By 2031, generative tools will fluently produce layout, imagery, and concept variations, and the rationale for a student to execute compositions by hand erodes sharply, because image and document generation are precisely the creative-production tasks task-exposure research classifies as positively exposed. The instrumental case shifts from producing artwork toward briefing, selecting, and critically evaluating machine output, a genuine change in what the course must impart. The foundational cap now expires, since scaffolding protection was near-term only, so the rating rises once diffusion catches capability. There is no embodiment here, the work being fully digital, and no accreditation or licensure mandate protects it. The residual value is the trained eye that catches a weak hierarchy or off-brand composition, echoing the jagged-frontier finding that unaided reliance on AI output degrades accuracy. That verification competence is real but narrower than the course's production-heavy content, which supports a High rather than Medium reading.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating publication-ready visual communication across print and screen from a brief, and the applied production tasks this course teaches are largely automated. GDPval-style evidence already shows models approaching, though not exceeding, human parity on real occupational deliverables, and creative production sits on the exposed side of that frontier. The instrumental need to learn to execute fundamental design manually is substantially eroded; what persists is design judgment, framing problems and evaluating fit to audience and message, held by fewer practitioners who supervise generation. No foundational cap, embodiment, or institutional lock binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine: ten-year forecasts carry wide uncertainty, and cultivated visual judgment could retain a stronger verification premium than a pure capability read implies. But relative to the catalog this is a clearly exposed production course whose instrumental necessity declines markedly, and the rating is High.
CDES 2222.d: Students in this course learn fundamental theories and principles of communication design for print and screen media as a means to solve problems visually. Emphasis is on idea generation, processes, and concepts that integrate the use of specific technologies. Within this context students investigate the role of design and how it informs contemporary culture. This is an Integrated Media course.

r: The course teaches typography as a functional visual language: setting and spacing type, building grid systems, and working with typographic anatomy, construction, and classification to communicate with sophistication. These are digital design-production tasks mapping to O*NET's Thinking Creatively and layout-specification activities, and they fall in the exposed band, since observed-usage data places creative and document-formatting generation among prominent AI applications and current tools already auto-set type on grids and generate typographic variants. The near-term rating is held to Medium by two facts: the course is foundational scaffolding required for upper-division typography study such as Typographic Aesthetics, so students need the fluency to specify and evaluate machine-set type, and diffusion still trails capability at under a fifth of firms. There is no licensure or accreditation course-mandate. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role, which keeps the fluency instrumentally necessary even as automated typesetting matures.

By 2031, layout engines and generative tools will competently set type, apply grid systems, and propose typographic hierarchies, weakening the rationale for students to execute this composition by hand; typographic production is exactly the creative-formatting work task-exposure research treats as positively exposed. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying intent and critically judging typographic fit rather than manually kerning and composing. Crucially, the foundational cap that protected the course near-term now lapses, so the rating rises as diffusion catches capability. No embodiment protects this fully digital craft, and no institutional mandate binds. What remains is the discriminating eye for legibility, rhythm, and appropriateness, a verification skill made more valuable by the jagged-frontier caution that plausible-looking but poorly composed output passes unnoticed without a trained reader. That residue is real yet narrower than the course's hands-on production content, supporting High.

A decade out, the central case has AI setting and refining typography to professional standard from a brief, and the manual composition tasks the course teaches are largely automated across print and screen. The instrumental need to learn to construct typographic systems by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is typographic judgment, deciding when a treatment serves the message and catching failures a model will not flag, held by fewer specialists. No foundational cap, embodiment, or licensure lock binds at this horizon, so nothing structurally preserves the course's necessity. The hedge is real, given ten-year forecasting uncertainty and the possibility that refined typographic sensibility commands a lasting verification premium as generation becomes ubiquitous. Even so, relative to the catalog this is a production course whose applied output sits squarely in the exposed creative categories, and its instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 2225.d: Students in this course are introduced to the study of typography focusing on the function of typography as a visual language, a form of communication, and a central theme in the field of communication design. Subjects explored include typographic history, anatomy, construction and design, grid systems, and identification and classification systems. Functional issues of setting and using typography with sophistication within a variety of contexts are central to this course.

r: Unlike the studio courses, Design Inquiry is a theory-and-writing course: students engage critical frameworks and readings, then assess how designed communications function as products, services, and experiences within social, economic, and environmental contexts, producing written and analytical outcomes. The applied tasks, critical reading and expository writing about design, map to O*NET's Getting Information and Interpreting the Meaning of Information activities and are among the most exposed in the evidence base, given controlled studies showing large AI writing gains and task-exposure research placing writing strongly on the positively exposed side. The near-term rating is capped at Medium by the course's foundational role introducing the discipline's vocabulary before upper-division study, and by adoption still lagging capability. There is no embodiment and no licensure lock. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role; the critical-reasoning core offers partial but not decisive protection, since the graded artifacts are largely text.

By 2031, language models will fluently generate design criticism and analytical essays on the cultural function of designed artifacts, sharply eroding the rationale for students to compose them; professional-writing RCTs already show roughly forty percent time savings with quality gains, and this course's output is squarely that kind of prose. The instrumental case shifts toward evaluating arguments and directing AI-drafted analysis rather than producing it, and the foundational cap that protected the course near-term now expires. No embodiment or institutional mandate binds. The residual competence is critical judgment, distinguishing a sound design argument from a fluent but shallow one, which the jagged-frontier evidence suggests grows more necessary as models produce plausible text that misleads unaided readers. That reasoning residue provides a modest hedge but not a binding constraint, since much of the course's assessed work is exactly the exposed writing task, so the rating rises to High.

A decade out, AI generates sophisticated design-theory analysis and criticism on demand, and the writing-and-interpretation tasks the course centers on are performed competently with limited human input. The instrumental need for a student to produce this analysis themselves is substantially eroded; what endures is the reader's own cultivated critical sensibility, which is largely an intrinsic aim this rating does not score, plus a narrower verification role in checking machine-generated claims about design's social impact. No foundational cap, embodiment, or transfer mandate binds at this horizon, so nothing structurally preserves necessity. The hedge is genuine, given both ten-year uncertainty and the chance that disciplined critical reasoning retains an oversight premium. But among communication-design offerings this theory course lacks the studio's craft protection and sits in the highly exposed writing categories, so its instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 2226.d: Students in this course are introduced to the fundamental theories, principles, and objectives of the communication design field. Critical frameworks presented in readings respond to historic and contemporary contexts that define design practice and its impacts. The function of designed communications as products, services, and experiences are assessed in their relationship to culture through social, economic, and environmental factors. Theoretical and practical content includes the role technology and audience experience play in a contemporary context where "design" is ubiquitous.

r: The course builds foundational interaction and interface competencies: constructing design processes and interactive systems, mapping components, and applying user-experience research plus usability and accessibility strategies to create digital experiences. These tasks map to O*NET's Working with Computers and Thinking Creatively activities and are highly exposed, since UI generation and code-adjacent design sit in the largest observed-usage category, Computer and Mathematical, and current tools already scaffold interfaces, flows, and accessible markup. The near-term rating stays Medium because the course is foundational scaffolding for advanced interactive study such as Interactive Design I, so students need the fundamentals to specify and verify generated interfaces, and because firm adoption remains under a fifth despite fast capability. No licensure or accreditation course-mandate applies. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role, which keeps the interaction fundamentals instrumentally necessary even as automated UI drafting and layout generation become competent and increasingly available.

By 2031, AI will competently generate interface layouts, interaction patterns, and accessible components from requirements, and even produce usability heuristics, eroding the rationale for students to construct these systems by hand; developer-productivity RCTs show speedups above fifty percent on comparable digital tasks. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying user needs, judging accessibility and usability, and validating generated interfaces rather than building them from scratch, and the foundational cap protecting the course near-term now lapses. There is no embodiment, the work being fully digital, and no institutional mandate. The residual value is user-centered judgment and the ability to catch where a generated flow fails real users, a verification competence the jagged-frontier evidence makes more, not less, necessary. That residue is real but narrower than the course's production content, so as diffusion catches capability the rating rises to High for this horizon.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating usable, accessible interfaces and interactive systems directly from goals and content, and the construction tasks this course teaches are largely automated. The instrumental need to learn to build foundational interaction design by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is UX judgment, deciding what to build and confirming it serves users, held by fewer designers supervising generation. No foundational cap, embodiment, or licensure lock binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine given ten-year uncertainty and the possibility that accessibility and usability verification retain a premium in high-stakes products where non-obvious failures carry real cost. Still, interface work sits in the single most exposed usage category, and F1 reaches its ceiling here as generative UI matures, so the instrumental case for the foundational course declines to High.
CDES 2302.d: Students in this course research and investigate various methods of constructing design processes and interactive systems for digital audiences. Students implement design frameworks and mapping for interactive components while gaining fundamental skills in user experience research and interaction design, including foundational user interface design competencies. Emphasis is placed on usability, accessibility and user-centered design strategies for creating foundational interactive experiences. This is an Integrated Media course.

r: The course combines interface design with actual web development: students author and produce a functioning website using intuitive UI tools and foundational web development, applying industry standards and procedures. This joins two of the most exposed activity classes, mapping to O*NET's Working with Computers and Interacting With Computers, since coding is the single largest observed-usage category and controlled studies show large developer speedups, while generative tools already scaffold and style working sites. The near-term rating is Medium, not higher, because the course is foundational scaffolding for advanced interactive and community-design coursework, so students need enough web fluency to direct and verify generated code, and because diffusion still trails capability across firms. No licensure or accreditation course-mandate binds. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role, which keeps front-end fundamentals instrumentally necessary even as AI competently produces functioning sites from descriptions and design references.

By 2031, AI will reliably generate, style, and debug functioning websites from a brief and a design, and the "hand-code the site yourself" rationale erodes substantially; developer-productivity evidence already shows task speedups above fifty percent, and GDPval-style results place models near human parity on real deliverables. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying, integrating, and verifying generated front-end work rather than authoring it, and the foundational cap protecting the course near-term now expires. There is no embodiment and no institutional mandate. The distinctive residue is the ability to read, test, and fix machine-generated code and to judge whether a site meets standards and accessibility, a verification skill the jagged-frontier finding makes essential, since developers who cannot check AI output ship unreliable work. That residue is genuine but narrower than the course's build-oriented content, so as adoption catches capability the rating rises to High.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing production-quality websites and interfaces directly from goals and content, and the development tasks this course teaches are largely automated. The instrumental need to learn foundational web construction by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is specification and verification, deciding what to build and confirming it works and meets standards, held by fewer practitioners overseeing generation. No foundational cap, embodiment, or licensure lock binds at this horizon, so nothing structurally preserves the course's necessity. The hedge is real, given ten-year forecasting uncertainty and the possibility that debugging and integration judgment retain an oversight premium as software self-generates. But web and interface work sits in the most exposed category in the entire evidence base, and F1 reaches its ceiling here, so the instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 2602.d: Students in this course examine contemporary standards of interactive web design and development. Students investigate contemporary design culture, conceptual development and technical learning capabilities with application to real-world scenarios based on industry expectations and procedures. As author and designer, students produce a functioning website utilizing the web as a vehicle for community-driven collaborations. Students gain knowledge of intuitive user interface design tools and foundational web development. This is an Integrated Media course.

r: The course centers on print publishing: editorial design and content development, print production and post-production, and self-publishing magazines and books, alongside distribution and the business of publishing on the collaborative Zeromile staff. The core applied tasks, editorial layout, copy development, and prepress preparation, map to O*NET's Thinking Creatively and layout-specification activities and are exposed, since observed-usage data places creative and office-document generation among prominent AI applications and tools already draft editorial layouts and long-form copy. The collaborative magazine role adds real in-person teamwork, but the graded design production is digital. There is no licensure, accreditation, or gen-ed mandate here, and the course is a fairly terminal upper-division elective rather than scaffolding for later required work. At 24 months the rating is Medium because near-term diffusion, under a fifth of firms, limits realized substitution even though the editorial-production tasks are competently automatable.

By 2031, generative tools will fluently produce editorial layouts, article drafts, and prepress-ready files, and the rationale for students to execute publication design by hand erodes; both the layout and the writing sit in the positively exposed creative and office categories that task-exposure research flags. The instrumental case shifts toward editorial direction, curation, and quality control of AI-produced pages rather than manual composition, and no protective factor binds, since embodiment is limited, there is no institutional lock, and the course is terminal rather than foundational. The residue is editorial judgment, deciding what to publish and catching where generated layout or copy misfires, a verification role the jagged-frontier evidence makes more valuable as fluent but flawed output proliferates. That residue is real but narrower than the course's production and post-production content, so the rating rises to High as adoption catches the already-present capability.

A decade out, AI competently generates editorial design, content, and print-ready output end to end, and the publishing-production tasks this course teaches are largely automated, with human effort concentrated in editorial vision, curation, and the interpersonal business of publishing. The instrumental need to learn to produce a magazine by hand is substantially eroded; what endures is judgment and the collaborative, presence-dependent parts of running a publication, which are a fraction of the course's design-production content. No foundational cap, embodiment sufficient to protect, or institutional mandate binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine given ten-year uncertainty and the chance that editorial taste retains a curatorial premium. But relative to the catalog this is an exposed creative-production course lacking the studio-craft or licensure protections that hold other offerings down, so its instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 3001.d: Students in this course examine communication design's role in print publishing. Zeromile is a self-funded, annual, print and Internet magazine published collectively by students and faculty in the Communication Design program. In addition to performing a staff role on Zeromile students self-publish their own magazines ('zines) and books. Topics include editorial design and content development, print publishing software and tools, print production and post-production techniques, copyright issues, publication, distribution and the business of publishing.

r: This course is distinguished from the program's studio-production offerings by sustained, real-time engagement with underserved communities: students work in teams directly with marginalized participants to co-develop design solutions addressing social, environmental, and economic problems, and are required to work in a highly inclusive manner with project participants. The design artifacts are exposed to generative production, but the assessed competence is participatory, relational, and partly embodied, mapping to O*NET's Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships and Communicating with People Outside the Organization, which task-exposure research places among the least automatable, high-presence categories. That in-person community-collaboration core triggers the embodiment dampener and holds the rating to Low at 24 months. There is no licensure lock; the protection is presence and the human judgment of assessing real people's needs, where errors carry welfare consequences. AI may draft candidate designs, but it does not conduct the community relationship the course builds.

By 2031, generative tools will readily produce the visual deliverables of public-interest projects, and AI will assist with research synthesis and communication, meaningfully augmenting rather than replacing the student designer, consistent with observed automation-versus-augmentation patterns that lean augmentative in professional settings. But the course's core, co-designing with communities through sustained interpersonal engagement and judging genuine human need in context, remains presence-dependent and carries a real verification burden because misreading a community's needs harms vulnerable people. Embodiment keeps the base rating dampened, yet with no foundational cap and no institutional mandate, the protection is the interpersonal core alone, which lifts the rating modestly to Medium as production tasks around that core automate. The instrumental need to develop participatory, community-facing design competence is not eliminated; what shifts is that more of the artifact production is machine-assisted while the human collaboration endures.

A decade out, AI will handle most of the production and much of the analytical work in community-based projects, and the designer's role concentrates further on the relational, ethically weighty engagement with participants. The embodied, in-person collaboration at the heart of the course resists direct substitution, and verifying that a solution truly fits a community's lived circumstances still requires a present human, so the rating holds at Medium rather than rising to High. There is no licensure or foundational cap doing this work; the protection is the interpersonal and presence-dependent core, which is genuine but surrounds an increasingly automated production shell. The hedge is real: ten-year uncertainty is wide, and the balance between automated deliverable generation and human community work could shift. But the participatory competence this course develops remains instrumentally necessary, distinguishing it sharply from the program's exposed studio courses.
CDES 3101.d: This course challenges students to formulate design solutions that create positive change collaboratively with underserved or marginalized communities and individuals. Sometimes referred to as design in the public interest, this course facilitates interaction between student designers and those in need of life-changing design solutions. Students work in teams to solve triple bottom line issues through social, environmental and economic filters. Emphasis is on development projects that can be implemented regionally, nationally or internationally. Students are required to work in a highly inclusive manner with project participants. This is an integrated media course.

r: The course pairs critical typographic analysis with production: students examine typographic form, function, and meaning across social and historical contexts and design custom typefaces while practicing conceptualization, authoring, and research. Typeface design and typographic composition are digital creative-production tasks mapping to O*NET's Thinking Creatively and layout-specification activities, and they fall in the exposed band, since generative and parametric type tools already produce and vary letterforms and observed usage places creative generation among common applications. The critical-analysis component is somewhat less automatable, offering partial protection. The near-term rating is Medium because the course is foundational scaffolding, a heavy prerequisite gate for much upper-division communication-design work, so students need the fluency to direct and evaluate generated type, and because adoption still trails capability. No licensure or accreditation course-mandate binds. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role, keeping the competence instrumentally necessary as automated type design matures.

By 2031, AI will competently generate and refine typefaces and typographic systems and even draft the analytical framing, eroding the rationale for students to produce this work by hand; type design sits in the positively exposed creative categories, and GDPval-style evidence shows models nearing human parity on real deliverables. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying, curating, and critically evaluating generated type rather than constructing it, and the foundational cap protecting the course near-term now lapses. There is no embodiment and no institutional mandate. The distinctive residue is the discriminating analytical judgment about meaning and appropriateness, a verification competence the jagged-frontier finding makes more necessary as fluent but ill-fitting type proliferates. That reasoning residue is genuine and stronger here than in purely mechanical production courses, but it is still narrower than the course's design-production content, so the rating rises to High as diffusion catches capability.

A decade out, the central case has AI designing custom typefaces and typographic systems to professional standard and generating sophisticated typographic criticism, so the applied production and much of the analysis this course teaches are largely automated. The instrumental need to learn to design type and compose typographically by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is refined critical judgment about typographic meaning and fit, held by fewer specialists who direct and verify generation. No foundational cap, embodiment, or licensure lock binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine, given ten-year uncertainty and the real possibility that deep typographic sensibility retains an oversight premium as generation becomes ubiquitous. Even so, this is a production-centered course whose applied output sits in the exposed creative categories, and its instrumental case declines to High, with the critical residue as the main hedge.
CDES 3215.d: Students in this course conduct critical studies of typographic design with an emphasis on the meaning, application, and aesthetics of typography solutions by examining typographic form, function, and concepts. Students analyze and criticize the meaning of typographic form in various social, cultural and historical communication contexts. Students construct and design custom typefaces while further practicing and analyzing critical conceptualization, authoring, and research skills.

r: The course teaches design research: applying methods like ethnographic strategies, personas, interviewing, and iterative processes to produce communications appropriate for specific audiences and contexts, with teamwork putting theory into practice. Much of the applied work, research synthesis, persona construction, and analysis, maps to O*NET's Getting Information and Analyzing Data or Information activities and is exposed, since AI competently retrieves, clusters, and summarizes qualitative material. Interviewing adds a partial interpersonal, primary-research element that is less automatable. The near-term rating is Medium because the course functions as a foundational research substrate taken alongside other required upper-division work, so students need the methods to design and verify AI-assisted research, and because diffusion still lags capability across firms. There is no licensure or accreditation course-mandate. The binding constraint at 24 months is the foundational-substrate role; the human primary-research element offers partial but not decisive protection given how automatable synthesis has become.

By 2031, AI will fluently conduct and synthesize secondary research, generate personas, and draft affinity analyses, substantially automating the desk-research execution this course teaches; analysis and writing tasks of this kind are broadly exposed. The instrumental case shifts toward framing research questions, conducting the human primary contact that interviews require, and critically validating machine-surfaced findings, and the foundational cap protecting the course near-term now expires. There is no strong embodiment, most work being analytical, and no institutional mandate. The distinctive residue is source evaluation and the detection of fabricated or misleading synthesis, a verification competence the jagged-frontier evidence makes essential, since models produce plausible research summaries that mislead unaided readers. That residue, together with the interpersonal interviewing element, provides a genuine hedge, but it is narrower than the course's synthesis-heavy content, so the rating rises to High as adoption catches capability.

A decade out, AI conducts and integrates design research at a high level, generating personas, synthesizing qualitative data, and drafting insights, so the research-execution tasks the course centers on are largely automated. The instrumental need to perform this synthesis by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is judgment about what to study, the conduct of genuinely human primary research, and rigorous verification of machine findings, held by fewer researchers directing the tools. No foundational cap, embodiment sufficient to protect, or licensure lock binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine: ten-year uncertainty is wide, and the interviewing and validation residue could retain a stronger premium than a pure capability read implies, especially where fabricated synthesis carries real cost. But the bulk of the course's applied work sits in exposed analytical categories, so its instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 3222.d: This course examines how designers conduct research in order to produce relevant and meaningful visual communications that are appropriate for specific audiences, cultures, and contexts. Students learn how to harness meaning and potential in their work by applying a range of research methods to their everyday design practice. Concepts include developing and using ethnographic strategies, personas, interviewing, and iterative design processes among others. Students work in teams, putting theory into action, which informs collaborative design practice thereafter.

r: Restricted to post-portfolio BFA majors, the course specializes in production technique: bridging design concepts and forms across print publishing, packaging, and product development through multi-level publishing, content management, production workflow, integrated software use, and print and new-media post-production. Some packaging and product elements have a physical facet, but the design and prepress core is digital. There is no licensure or accreditation course-mandate, and the course is a fairly terminal upper-division elective. At 24 months the rating is Medium because near-term diffusion, under a fifth of firms, limits realized substitution even as the production tasks are competently automatable.

By 2031, AI and workflow automation will competently execute layout, imposition, content assembly, and cross-media production preparation, eroding the rationale for students to master these techniques by hand; GDPval-style evidence shows models nearing human parity on real deliverables, and document production sits on the exposed side of that frontier. The instrumental case shifts toward specifying and quality-checking automated production rather than performing it, and with no foundational cap, no protective embodiment, and no institutional mandate, little restrains the rating. The residue is production judgment, catching where an automated file will fail on press or in fabrication, a verification role the jagged-frontier evidence makes valuable but which is narrower than the course's execution-heavy content. As diffusion catches the already-present capability, the rating rises to High for this horizon, the exposed digital-production core being the binding factor.

A decade out, the central case has AI and automated pipelines performing most cross-media production preparation, from multi-format layout to prepress and content management, so the technique-execution tasks this course teaches are largely automated. The instrumental need to learn integrated production by hand is substantially eroded; what persists is oversight judgment and the residual physical facets of packaging and product realization, a fraction of the course's digital-production content. No foundational cap, embodiment sufficient to protect, or licensure lock binds at this horizon. The hedge is genuine given ten-year uncertainty and the chance that production troubleshooting retains a verification premium where physical output carries cost. But this is by design a production-technique course whose applied output sits squarely in the exposed creative and office categories, so its instrumental case declines to High, F1 reaching its ceiling as automation matures.
CDES 3225.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 3 to 4. Explicitly focused on production techniques: production workflow, integrated software use, and print and new-media production and post-production. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections name generative AI as possibly limiting demand across arts, design, and media occupations (graphic designers -1.7%), and Strada's May 2026 employer survey reports AI reducing entry-level marketing and content work. CDES 3225.d: Students in this course are offered a specialized focus on production techniques integral to the practice of communication design. The application of integrated methods bridges design concepts and design forms in a variety of mediums including traditional print publishing, packaging, and product development. Students examine multi-level publishing, content management, production workflow, integrated software use, and print and new media production and post-production. This course is restricted to Communication Design majors who have passed the BFA in Communication Design portfolio review.

r: The course teaches experimental 2D and 3D digital animation, emphasizing innovative concepts and processes to expand animation forms within studio art. The experimental, conceptual emphasis offers some protection because unusual aesthetic intent is harder to specify, but the execution is automatable. There is no embodiment sufficient to dampen the rating, no licensure lock, and the course is a terminal elective. At 24 months the rating is Medium because near-term diffusion still trails the fast capability curve even as generative animation tools become competent at motion and form.

By 2031, generative animation tools will produce sophisticated 2D and 3D motion from prompts and references, eroding the rationale for students to execute experimental animation by hand; the rapid capability trend and GDPval-style parity results both point to competent automated production of exactly this creative output. The residue is the experimental conceptual vision and the eye to judge whether generated motion realizes an unusual intent, a curatorial and verification role that is genuine but narrower than the course's production content. As diffusion catches capability, the rating rises to High; the distinction from embodied studio art, which this course lacks, is what leaves it exposed.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating experimental animation across 2D and 3D to a high aesthetic standard from conceptual direction, so the production tasks this course teaches are largely automated. The instrumental need to learn to animate by hand is substantially eroded; the durable competence is conceptual originality and the judgment to direct and evaluate generated motion, held by fewer artists supervising tools. No foundational cap, physical embodiment, or licensure lock binds at this horizon, so nothing structurally preserves the course's necessity. The hedge is genuine, given wide ten-year uncertainty and the possibility that genuinely experimental aesthetic vision resists specification longer than routine production. But unlike physically embodied studio art, digital animation sits in the exposed creative-production categories on a fast capability trend, and F1 reaches its ceiling here, so the instrumental case declines to High.
CDES 3236.d: Students in this course learn experimental concepts and techniques to create 2D and 3D digital animations. They focus on the intellectual investigation of animation themes and forms, emphasizing innovative concepts and processes to expand the scope of animation possibilities within the discipline of studio art. This is an integrated media course.

r: Digital Illustration develops character design, concept art, and sequential art through immersive projects, with connections to animation and graphic design. Though hands-on, the craft is executed on screen, so it lacks the physical-psychomotor protection that shields painting. There is no licensure lock and the course is a terminal elective, so no institutional or foundational cap binds. The near-term rating is nonetheless Medium rather than High because realized adoption still lags the fast capability curve, with under a fifth of firms using AI by end-2025, and near-horizon substitution is partial even where studios already lean heavily on generative concept work.

By 2031, generative image tools will produce publication-ready character designs, concept art, and sequential panels from briefs, and the rationale for students to execute illustration by hand erodes markedly; this is the clearest case among design offerings where the applied output sits at the center of what image models already do well, with GDPval-style evidence showing models nearing human parity on real deliverables. The instrumental case shifts toward art direction, iteration, and curation of generated imagery rather than manual rendering, and with no foundational, embodiment, or institutional cap, little restrains the rating. The residue is compositional and narrative judgment and the ability to specify and refine a distinctive visual voice, a verification and direction role that is genuine but narrower than the course's production content. CDES 4251.d: Students in this course learn that good design can serve to enrich the human experience. Students explore a spectrum of life experiences and/or personal events, which may include habit, memory, disaster, and imagination, as inspiration to create and implement positive design solutions. Students produce a series of intensive, multi layered projects with emphasis on tracking, recording, and journaling the human experience. Students build upon their knowledge of design discourse in the discipline through a mix of readings, writings, and development of rich, meaningful design projects. Design projects are presented in a variety of media. This is an integrated media course.

r: The applied work is creating mobile applications through UX and UI design and interactive prototyping—usability, accessibility, user-centered methods, mobile strategy, and testing to build working design systems. Medium.

By 2031, AI prototyping and UI-generation tools will fluently produce mobile interfaces, component systems, and interactive flows from prompts, automating most of the production this course teaches. A decade out, the central case has AI generating mobile prototypes and design systems end to end, so the instrumental need to acquire hand-prototyping competence is substantially eroded. With no accreditation or licensure brake and fully digital deliverables, little protects the production. High.
CDES 4252.d: Students in this course create mobile applications via user experience, user interface design, and interactive prototyping. Exploration and emphasis is placed upon usability, accessibility as well as user-centered design methodologies and processes in this growing digital medium. Students utilize design thinking to better respond to diverse audiences, implement mobile strategy and content in order to create a working design system for mobile applications, inclusive of prototyping and testing. Human-centered design, dependent on the psychology and intersection of usability within digital mediums, is discussed, evaluated and applied to interactive prototyping in response to technology's continual diversification of end-user products.

r: The applied work is advanced thematic design production—developing critical and technical skills and a visual language responsive to a rotating topic, with projects realized across varied design applications. Holding the near-term rating below High is uneven adoption and the thematic critical framing that rewards human judgment. By 2031, generative design tools will fluently produce thematic visual work—concepts, compositions, and production files—across most applications a variable-topics course might cover, automating the bulk of production. Productivity research shows large creative-work gains, and observed-usage data places visual and writing tasks among prominent uses. Because the content varies by offering, the precise exposure is uncertain, but the production core is broadly automatable. A decade out, the central case has AI generating thematic communication design across applications, so the instrumental need to acquire the production competence is substantially eroded. No accreditation or licensure brake exists, and deliverables are digital, so embodiment offers little protection. What remains is the human's conceptual framing of a theme and the judgment to verify automated output—a narrowing function. The generic, rotating nature of the course makes any specific forecast uncertain, but the direction is clear: routine thematic production automates. Because the offering rotates, some future topics could emphasize less-exposed conceptual or research work while others center squarely on automatable making, so the true ten-year exposure depends on curricular choices not fixed in the catalog. High, with a wide band reflecting both content variability and the hard-to-forecast status of creative judgment; confidence is lower here than for well-specified courses in the batch.
CDES 4300.d: This course provides a thematic forum in communication design for advanced-level students to develop critical and technical skills as they relate to contemporary design practices. Exploration within the theme focuses on developing skills that communicate to diversified communities and are relevant to contemporary design culture. Students foster a visual language that reflects thematic course content. Projects may be produced in a variety of design applications based on course content. Variable topics: may be repeated for up to 9 credits under different topics.

r: The applied work is developing a thesis topic—conducting research, crafting a research question, refining an abstract, and creating visual studies of a project concept for a later exhibition. These map to O*NET Getting Information, Analyzing Information, Thinking Creatively, and Documenting/Recording Information. Task-exposure research classifies research synthesis and academic writing among positively exposed activities, and AI already drafts research questions, abstracts, and literature framing competently; productivity RCTs on professional writing show roughly 40% time savings and quality gains. Nothing binding protects the course—no licensure, accreditation, or general-studies lock—though it does scaffold the capstone in CDES 4721. Holding the near-term rating below High is uneven adoption and the fact that the thesis concept must be the student's own defensible investigation, which rewards original judgment and verification that AI-surfaced material is sound. Medium.

By 2031, AI research assistants will fluently retrieve sources, propose research questions, draft abstracts, and frame project concepts, automating much of the preparatory work this course grades. Observed-usage data places writing and analytic tasks among the most prominent applications, and capability trends point to continued gains. With only a scaffolding role and no institutional lock, nothing caps the erosion. The distinctive residue is the student's ownership of an original thesis direction and the judgment to evaluate and verify AI-surfaced claims—models fabricate plausibly, so the jagged-frontier caution applies to research framing directly. That verification-and-ownership residue keeps the competence useful, but the drafting core automates. High, hedged on how much original research framing genuinely resists capable tools.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently conducting and drafting research framing—questions, abstracts, and concept studies—so the execution the course teaches is largely automatable. With no accreditation or licensure brake and digital deliverables, little protects the work beyond the student's need to own and defend an original thesis downstream. What remains is the capacity to direct research, judge originality and soundness, and verify AI output—a shrinking but real function that also feeds the capstone in CDES 4721. The honest uncertainty is how thesis preparation is taught and assessed under ubiquitous AI research tools, and whether crafting a genuinely original investigation resists the fabrication-prone tools that make verification necessary, not whether routine framing automates; the evidence indicates it does. High.
CDES 4400.d: Students in this course develop a thesis topic supported by a research question, which serves as the foundation for a thesis project exhibition in CDES 4721 the following semester. Students conduct research, propose a topic for investigation, craft a research question, refine an abstract, and create visual studies of a project concept in an exhibition context. This course is restricted to Communication Design majors.

r: The applied work spans resume and application-material development, best practices for contract and freelance work, client pitching, networking, interviewing, workplace ethics, and entrepreneurial tasks like bidding and contract negotiation. These map to O*NET Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization, Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, and Documenting/Recording Information. Much of the document work—resumes, proposals, bid materials—is highly exposed writing; observed-usage data shows office and writing tasks are prominent AI applications, and RCTs report large writing gains. Nothing binding protects the course—no licensure or accreditation—though it scaffolds the internship and portfolio courses. Holding the near-term rating below High is uneven adoption and the live interpersonal core—pitching, networking, interviewing—that is real-time and only partly digital, keeping human competence necessary in that slice. Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently draft resumes, freelance proposals, bids, and client-pitch decks, automating most of the document-production side of professional practice. Productivity research on professional writing shows roughly 40% time savings and quality gains, and observed-usage data places such office tasks among prominent uses. With no institutional lock and only a modest scaffolding role, nothing caps erosion of the writing tasks. The residue is the interpersonal, real-time competence—actually pitching a concept to a client, negotiating a contract, interviewing—which tools coach but do not perform, and the ethical judgment the course teaches. That live-practice residue is genuine, but the balance of gradeable tasks tilts toward the automatable. High, hedged because the interpersonal and negotiation core is more resistant than the surrounding document work.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating professional documents—applications, proposals, bids, pitch materials—competently, so that side of the course's instrumental value is substantially eroded. No licensure or accreditation brake exists. What remains most durable is the embodied, real-time professional conduct—client relationships, negotiation, interviewing, and ethical judgment in practice—which is less exposed, though tools increasingly support even these. The honest uncertainty is how much of professional practice reduces to automatable artifacts versus irreducibly human relationship work; the course mixes both, and the writing-heavy majority automates. Even the pitching and negotiation slices face capable AI coaching and, in some channels, AI intermediaries, though the live, high-stakes human moments resist substitution longest. High, with a meaningful hedge reflecting the interpersonal residue that keeps some competence necessary through 2036.
CDES 4450.d: Students in this course are provided an overview of professional practices in communication design. Professional practices range from resume writing and job application material development to best practices in conducting contract and freelance work and pitching concepts in front of clients. Topics include strategies for personal communications packages, networking, applying for jobs, interviewing skills, and ethical practices in the work place as a design employee or proprietor in a wide variety of workplace settings. Entrepreneurial initiatives are covered from starting a business to negotiating contract and/or freelance work and bidding on jobs. This course is restricted to communication design majors.

r: The applied work is refining an existing body of design work into final portfolio solutions—clarifying project outcomes, redeveloping work as needed, and presenting it in web and print portfolios with supporting writing and critical inquiry. These map to O*NET Thinking Creatively, Analyzing Information, Documenting/Recording Information, and Drafting/Laying Out visual work. Both the design refinement and the portfolio writing are exposed: observed-usage data places writing and visual production among prominent AI uses, and generative tools build portfolio sites and draft project statements competently. Nothing binding protects the course—no licensure, accreditation, or general-studies lock—though it feeds the senior capstone. Holding the near-term rating below High is uneven adoption and the fact that the portfolio must represent the student's own demonstrated competence, which rewards personal curatorial judgment. Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently assemble portfolio websites, lay out print portfolios, and draft the critical writing that frames them, automating most of the production this course grades. Productivity research on professional writing shows large gains, and web-build tooling is among the most-exposed software work in observed usage. With no institutional lock and only a scaffolding role, nothing caps the erosion. The residue is curatorial and evaluative—selecting and sequencing one's strongest work, articulating its value authentically, and verifying that automated presentation actually represents the student's competence rather than a templated generic. That judgment persists, but the making of the portfolio artifact automates. High, hedged on how much self-curatorial judgment genuinely resists tools that increasingly template professional presentation.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating polished portfolios—web and print—and their supporting statements on demand, so the production competence the course builds is largely automatable. With no accreditation or licensure brake and digital deliverables, little protects the artifact-making. What remains is the reflective judgment about which work best demonstrates one's ability and how to frame it—a narrowing function, and one complicated by the fact that AI increasingly produces the underlying work being showcased—if the portfolio pieces are themselves AI-generated, the exercise's meaning shifts from demonstrating making toward demonstrating direction and taste. The honest uncertainty is how portfolio pedagogy adapts when presentation is automated, not whether the production automates; the evidence indicates it does. High.
CDES 4600.d: Students refine an existing body of work to generate final portfolio solutions. Students explore the critical nature of their work by clarifying project results, and as necessary, redeveloping outcomes, for presentation in both web and print-based portfolios. Writing and critical inquiry skills supporting portfolio development are emphasized. The portfolio work generated in this course will be used in the course CDES 4721 - Communication Design Senior Experience: Exhibition and Thesis.

r: The applied work is a supervised communication-design internship requiring at least 150 contact hours in a real workplace, applying classroom knowledge to professional challenges. The instrumental competence is the embodied, situated experience itself—operating inside a functioning design organization, meeting real deadlines and clients, and being professionally socialized. These map to O*NET Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships, Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization, and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public. Task-exposure research and observed-usage data both place in-person, relational work among the least automatable categories; an AI cannot undergo an internship on a student's behalf. The 150-contact-hour requirement functions as a structural clock that no capability advance satisfies. At 24 months the instrumental need for real-world professional experience is wholly intact. Low.

By 2031, AI will be pervasive inside the design workplaces where students intern, changing what interns do day to day—more direction of tools, less manual production. But that reshapes the content of the experience rather than removing the need for it: the course's value is situated professional socialization, real-time collaboration, and workplace judgment that only in-person presence builds. Observed-usage data shows relational and in-person work resists automation, and no tool substitutes for the lived experience of holding a role. The contact-hour structure persists across a catalog cycle. The instrumental case is essentially intact; interns increasingly supervise AI, but the experiential requirement does not automate, and the course's binding constraint is embodiment rather than any regulatory lock. Low.

A decade out, even with AI deeply embedded in design practice, the purpose of an internship—acquiring embodied professional experience, relationships, and situated judgment inside a real organization—remains something no model performs for the student. The tasks an intern handles will shift substantially toward oversight of automated production, and the field's labor market is genuinely uncertain over this horizon. But the instrumental need for supervised, in-person professional experience is not eroded by capability growth; embodiment, the relationships it builds, and the contact-hour structure hold it. Low, with the caveat that what students do during the internship changes more than whether they still need one—the experiential requirement is protected by presence, not by anything a capability advance can reach.
CDES 4625.d: Students in this course apply for and acquire a communication design internship identified for its professional challenges and overall integrity. Students gain "real world" experiences in the discipline of design building upon previous knowledge gained in the classroom. Fieldwork requires a minimum of 150 contact hours for three semester credit hours. This course is restricted to communication design majors. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: The applied work is functioning as a real design studio—students collaborate with faculty, peers, and university or community sponsors to take sponsored projects from planning through production and implementation per a design brief, across at least 150 contact hours, fulfilling the internship requirement. This mixes exposed design production with embodied, collaborative, real-time client work. It maps to O*NET Thinking Creatively and Drafting/Laying Out visual work alongside Establishing Interpersonal Relationships and Communicating with Persons Outside the Organization. Generative tools increasingly produce the design deliverables; observed-usage data places such production among prominent uses. But the studio's collaborative, client-facing, mentored experience is only partly digital. Holding the rating at Medium is that mixture—production automates, but the situated professional practice and the 150-contact-hour structure do not. Medium.

By 2031, generative tools will handle much of the design production sponsored studio projects require—concepts, layouts, production files—automating a substantial share of the deliverable work. Productivity research shows large creative-work gains and observed-usage data places design among prominent applications. Yet Studio M's instrumental core is experiential and collaborative: managing real sponsor relationships, working a brief in a team under mentorship, and delivering to a live client. That embodied professional practice, plus the contact-hour structure, resists automation even as production does not. The rating holds Medium: the making automates, but the situated studio competence remains. Hedged on how quickly client-facing studio work reorganizes around AI tools and how much of the collaborative practice stays human.

A decade out, the central case has AI producing most of the design deliverables sponsored studio work entails, so the production rationale is substantially eroded. What endures is the collaborative, client-facing professional experience—running real projects with sponsors under mentorship—that the course exists to provide and that no model undergoes for the student. As production automates, the studio's value concentrates in that experiential, relational judgment and in directing and verifying automated output. The rating rises to High because the gradeable design production is largely automatable by 2036, though the experiential residue is real and the forecast for collaborative client work is genuinely uncertain; how much a sponsor still values a human-run studio over an AI-assisted solo practitioner is precisely the open question the decade will answer. High.
CDES 4650.d: This course operates as a functioning design studio where communication design students work collaboratively with course faculty and peers and a range of university and/or community sponsors. Sponsored projects are taken from initiation and planning through to final production and implementation based on the requirements of the design brief. This unique mentored opportunity requires students to apply for a limited number of available design positions in Studio M. Studio M requires a minimum of 150 contact hours for three semester hours. The course fulfills the senior level internship requirement in the Communication Design major.

r: The applied work is the BFA capstone: creating a thesis design project, researching and writing a thesis paper, mounting a public exhibition, and defending the work in a formal review, plus team organization of the exhibition. This maps to O*NET Thinking Creatively, Getting Information, Documenting/Recording Information, and Performing for or Working Directly with the Public. The thesis design and paper are exposed—generative tools draft visual work and academic prose, per productivity research showing large writing gains—but the capstone's core is integrative and embodied: synthesizing a program of study, publicly exhibiting, and defending original work live. Nothing binding protects it institutionally, yet the exhibition and oral defense are real-time and personal. Holding the near-term rating at Medium is that mixture of exposed production and non-automatable synthesis, presentation, and defense. Medium.

By 2031, AI will fluently draft thesis papers and generate design work, automating much of the artifact production a capstone requires. Observed-usage data places writing and visual tasks among prominent applications. Yet the capstone's instrumental purpose is to demonstrate integrated competence through a public exhibition and a live defense of original work—activities that are embodied, real-time, and verification-heavy, since the point is proving the student's own capability rather than producing a deliverable. That defense-and-exhibition core resists automation even as drafting does not. The rating holds Medium: the producible artifacts are increasingly automatable, but the synthesizing, presenting, and defending are not. Hedged on how much of the thesis reduces to automatable output versus irreducible demonstration.

A decade out, the central case has AI competently producing thesis-grade design work and written papers, so the artifact side of the capstone is largely automatable. What endures is the integrative demonstration—publicly exhibiting and defending an original body of work as evidence of the student's own competence—which no model performs for them, and which carries a genuine verification function. As production automates, the capstone's value concentrates there. The rating rises to High because the gradeable production is broadly automatable by 2036, though the embodied exhibition-and-defense residue keeps some competence necessary and the forecast for integrative creative judgment is uncertain. Much depends on whether programs redesign the capstone around live demonstration precisely because the artifacts are automatable, which would preserve its instrumental point even as production erodes. High.
CDES 4721.d: Students in this BFA in Communication Design capstone course create a thesis project, research and write a thesis paper, participate in a public exhibition, and defend their work in a formal, final review setting. Students synthesize learning from previous coursework and articulate meaning in their thesis investigations relative to art and design theories, movements, and conceptual and philosophical frameworks. Students work in teams to conceptualize, organize, and present an exhibition consisting of the work of participating art and design students. A blend of team and individual activities punctuate the semester experience culminating in the public thesis exhibition.

r: The applied work is embodied studio support: assisting in laboratories, maintaining tools and equipment, mixing chemicals where appropriate, handling and stocking supplies, and demonstrating techniques to other students. These map to O*NET Handling and Moving Objects, Performing General Physical Activities, and Controlling Machines and Processes. Task-exposure research consistently places manual and physical work among the least automatable categories, strongly negatively associated with AI exposure; observed-usage data shows physical tasks least represented in actual use. No model maintains a press, mixes a chemical, or stocks a studio, and the peer demonstration is in-person. There is no licensure lock, but embodiment is the binding constraint. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on studio-support competence is wholly intact. Low.

By 2031, AI will assist with scheduling, inventory tracking, or documentation around a studio, but the core work—physically maintaining equipment, handling materials, and demonstrating technique in person—remains outside what models perform. Task-exposure research places manual and psychomotor work firmly in the low-exposure range, and robotics diffusion into small academic studios is negligible on this horizon. Verification and safety around chemicals and equipment further require a knowledgeable human physically present. The instrumental case is essentially intact: administrative edges may automate, but the embodied studio competence does not, and the safety-critical handling of equipment and chemicals actively demands a trained human on site rather than an automated recommendation. Low, since manual maintenance, material handling, and in-person technique demonstration stay firmly beyond the reach of language and reasoning models across this horizon.

A decade out, more studio administration could automate, and physical automation in industrial settings will advance materially. But the pedagogical function here—a student personally acquiring hands-on competence in maintaining tools, handling materials safely, and demonstrating technique to peers—is not eliminated by that trend, and embodiment keeps direct substitution low in an academic studio. The central case still has assistants doing physical, in-person work, both because the equipment is manual and because the safety dimension keeps a knowledgeable human on site. Employers and instructors continue to expect demonstrated hands-on facility with studio tools and materials, which no model supplies to the learner. Low, with the acknowledgment that documentation and inventory tasks around the role are the most plausible thing to shift, not the embodied competence itself.
CDES 4801.d: This studio course allows the advanced student to put into use the studio skills learned in previous courses to assist faculty and other students. Students learn to assist in laboratories, maintain tools and equipment, mix chemicals (if appropriate) and handle and stock supplies in an appropriate manner. They demonstrate techniques and assist other students with technical and creative questions.

r: The applied work is embodied traditional craft: operating letterpress equipment, maintaining letterpress tools and presses, handling inks, stocking supplies, and demonstrating printing technique to less-experienced students. These map to O*NET Handling and Moving Objects, Controlling Machines and Processes, and Performing General Physical Activities. This is precisely the manual, psychomotor work task-exposure research classifies as least exposed and strongly negatively associated with AI; observed-usage data shows physical tasks least represented in actual use. No model operates a press, mixes ink, or teaches inking pressure by hand. There is no licensure lock, but the craft's embodiment is an absolute binding constraint. At 24 months the instrumental need to acquire hands-on letterpress competence is wholly intact. Low.

By 2031, AI may support design of what gets printed, but the letterpress operation itself—setting, inking, adjusting impression, maintaining presses, and demonstrating these physically—remains outside what any model performs. Task-exposure research places such manual craft firmly in the low-exposure range, and robotics has no meaningful path into hand letterpress instruction on this horizon. Diffusion data showing uneven, capability-lagging adoption is largely beside the point here, because the constraint is physical rather than a matter of deployment. The instrumental case is intact; if anything, the deliberately traditional, apprenticeship-style transmission of press craft is among the least exposed activities in the catalog. Nothing in the capability trajectory—faster models, longer task horizons, better image generation—reaches the act of physically operating and maintaining a press. Low.

A decade out, even with pervasive AI in design and some industrial print automation, the specific competence here—hand operation and maintenance of letterpress equipment, transmitted through in-person demonstration—is not a task AI executes for the student. Embodiment is the whole point; the craft is valued partly for being manual and human-passed. The central case still has assistants learning and teaching press work physically, both because the equipment is manual and because the pedagogical aim is the transmission of embodied technique from more to less experienced hands. Low, with a narrow uncertainty band: this is close to the least automatable competence a communication-design program offers, and nothing on the capability trajectory reaches it.
CDES 4802.d: This studio course allows the advanced student to put into use letterpress printing operation and skills learned in previous courses and through specialized training workshops to assist faculty and other students. Students learn to assist in laboratories, maintain letterpress tools and equipment, and handle inks and stock supplies in an appropriate manner. They demonstrate techniques and assist other students with technical and creative questions.

r: The applied work is advanced independent studio production—integrating prior techniques to produce finished work for portfolio or thesis, developing an individual voice and a coherent body of work; the required student laptop signals digital production. These map to O*NET Thinking Creatively, Drafting/Laying Out visual work, and Interacting With Computers. Task-exposure research places digital design production among positively exposed activities, and generative tools already draft concepts, imagery, and layouts competently; GDPval shows models approaching half of expert-level deliverable quality. By 2031, generative design tools will fluently produce finished visual work—concepts, imagery, production files—so the independent production this course grades is largely automatable. With no institutional lock and no foundational role, nothing caps the erosion. That personal-direction residue keeps the competence useful while the making automates. High, hedged on how much individuated creative judgment resists increasingly capable tools.

A decade out, the central case has AI generating finished communication-design work on demand, so the independent-production competence the course builds is largely automatable. With no accreditation or licensure brake and digital deliverables, embodiment offers little protection. What remains is the development of a distinctive personal voice and the judgment to direct and verify automated output toward a coherent body of work—a narrowing function as tools improve at stylistic range and can increasingly mimic a specified voice. The honest uncertainty is whether individuated artistic judgment stays predominantly human, not whether routine production automates; the evidence favors broad automation of the making, leaving direction and selection as the durable human contribution. High.
CDES 4842.d: This course provides advanced, independent studio work in communication design with emphasis on the production of finished work in preparation for either senior portfolio or thesis exhibition. The student integrates techniques and skills learned in previous courses to develop an individual voice and create a coherent body of work.

r: The applied work is advanced independent letterpress production through an apprenticeship model—producing finished printed work, becoming familiar with type and presses through ongoing maintenance, handling inks and supplies, and assisting in the lab. These map to O*NET Handling and Moving Objects, Controlling Machines and Processes, and Performing General Physical Activities. The independent, finished-work emphasis still resolves to physical output produced by the student's own hands at the press. A decade out, even with pervasive AI in design and some industrial print automation, the specific competence—hand production and press maintenance transmitted through apprenticeship—is not a task AI executes for the student. The central case still has students producing letterpress work physically, and the apprenticeship structure explicitly values knowledge passed hand to hand from more to less experienced practitioners, a mode of learning that presupposes physical co-presence at the press. Low, with a narrow and confident uncertainty band: this sits at the least-automatable end of the communication-design catalog, where the value is explicitly in the manual, human-passed craft, untouched by advances in generative tools.
CDES 4848.d: Students in this course create advanced, independent studio work in communication design with emphasis on the production of finished work in letterpress printing through an emulation of the traditional Letterpress apprenticeship model in which knowledge is continually passed on to those with less experience. Skills learned in previous courses and through specialized training workshops are used to produce advanced studio work. Students become familiar with type and presses through ongoing maintenance training and activities. Students learn to assist in laboratories, maintain letterpress tools and equipment, handle inks and supplies in an appropriate manner. They demonstrate techniques and assist other students with technical and creative questions.
